comment_text:
This advice is honestly pretty bad; some of it even contradicts itself. I’ve been interested in human behavior and relationships since I was a teenager, and while a few of these ideas might seem to “work” when you’re young, they miss something fundamental.

The biggest flaw is the assumption about who is being “seduced.” It frames attraction like one person is targeting someone who’s missing something. That’s not only unhealthy, it’s not someone you should be seeking out in the first place.

If you actually want to attract people, the formula is much simpler and a lot more grounded: have real interests, develop your values, build a life you’re proud of, and pursue hobbies you genuinely enjoy. Then find someone whose values align with yours and who shares some of those interests. That’s where real connection comes from.

Also, this idea that one person is doing all the “seducing” is just wrong. Relationships aren’t one-sided strategies; they require mutual interest and effort. It takes two people who both want to build something together. If it feels like a game, you’ve already lost. That is unless you are specifically seeking out not the brightest humans lol. I personally am attracted to anxious nerdy/smart women. People emotionally intelligent will know the act, and see it as a red flag. I sure would. 

And a lot of the examples used to justify this kind of advice aren’t exactly reliable; many involve people with extreme privilege or behavior that’s honestly a bit unhinged. That’s not a blueprint for a healthy relationship.

Get to know who you are, and treat yourself like a commodity that needs to grow. People will absolutely show up to invest in something that looks like it will be something successful. Most people eventually go through the motion of imagining waking up next to the person for the rest of their life. We all do. You just need to be someone another person would like to see every day. 

When I met my wife, we never stopped seeing each other after that first date. For years, we didn’t even go a single day apart. We’ve been together 14 years now, and she’s still my best friend.

The point is simple: stop playing games. Take care of yourself first, build a life you’re proud of, and then show up for the people you genuinely want to invest in INCLUDING PLATONIC relationships. Real relationships aren’t built on strategy, they’re built on consistency, mutual effort, and actually caring about each other.
